title: Introduction
description: SwiftPieces is the central place for animated SwiftUI pieces. Copy one file, run one command, or let your agent install it.

contents.content: SwiftPieces is a free library (MIT + Commons Clause) of animated SwiftUI components built around iOS 26 Liquid Glass and Metal shaders, and a curated taste of what SwiftPieces Pro offers in full: production-ready SwiftUI screens and complete app templates. Read why SwiftPieces exists and how it is funded.

title: SwiftUI Liquid Glass guide (iOS 26)
description: How to use Liquid Glass in SwiftUI with glassEffect, GlassEffectContainer and glassEffectID, and how to fall back to Material below iOS 26.

contents.content: Liquid Glass shipped with iOS 26. The APIs are small, but the failure modes are not: glass sampling glass, missing fallbacks, invented modifiers from tutorials. Every glass piece here follows the same rules.

contents.heading: the-rules
contents.content: **Gate it.** `if #available(iOS 26, *)` around every glass call, with a `Material` fallback in the `else` branch.

contents.heading: the-rules

contents.heading: the-rules

contents.heading: the-rules
contents.content: **Glass goes last.** Apply `.glassEffect` after layout and appearance modifiers.

contents.heading: the-rules
contents.content: **Morph with IDs.** Pair `.glassEffectID(_:in:)` with a `@Namespace` to animate between shapes on state change.

contents.heading: the-rules
contents.content: **Only real APIs.** `.liquidGlassUltra`, `.fill(.liquidGlass)` and friends do not exist. The pieces here are type-checked against the SDK in CI.

title: SwiftUI Animations: A Practical Guide with Examples
description: SwiftUI animations explained with working examples: implicit and explicit animation, spring animation, transitions, keyframe animators, and gestures.

contents.content: SwiftUI animations work by interpolating between two states of your view: you change some state, and SwiftUI animates every property that depends on it from the old value to the new one. You choose *when* to animate (implicitly with `.animation(_:value:)` or explicitly with `withAnimation`) and *how* to animate (a spring, an easing curve, or a keyframe timeline).

This guide covers the full toolkit on iOS 17: springs, transitions, `matchedGeometryEffect`, phase and keyframe animators, numeric text, scroll-driven effects, gesture-driven motion that keeps the finger's velocity, and Reduce Motion. Every snippet compiles against the iOS 17 SDK.

contents.heading: implicit-vs-explicit-animation
contents.content: An **implicit** animation is attached to a view and fires whenever a specific value changes.

contents.heading: implicit-vs-explicit-animation
contents.content: Always pass `value:`. The old `.animation(_:)` without a value animates every change that reaches the view, including ones you did not mean to animate, and it is deprecated.

contents.heading: implicit-vs-explicit-animation
contents.content: An **explicit** animation wraps the state change itself. Everything that changes as a result of that mutation animates, anywhere in the hierarchy.

contents.heading: implicit-vs-explicit-animation
contents.content: A good rule: use `withAnimation` for user actions (a tap, a submit, a selection) and implicit animation for values that change on their own (a model update, a timer). On iOS 17, `withAnimation(_:completionCriteria:_:completion:)` also gives you a completion callback, which replaces most `DispatchQueue.main.asyncAfter` hacks.

contents.heading: spring-animations
contents.content: Springs are the default in modern SwiftUI, and they should be your default too. A spring is described by two numbers:

contents.heading: spring-animations
contents.content: `duration`: how long the motion feels, not a hard stop time.

contents.heading: spring-animations
contents.content: `bounce`: 0 is critically damped (no overshoot), 0.1 to 0.3 is a gentle overshoot, higher values wobble. Negative values are overdamped.

contents.heading: spring-animations
contents.content: SwiftUI ships three presets that cover most interface work:

contents.heading: spring-animations
contents.content: Preset

contents.heading: spring-animations
contents.content: Feel

contents.heading: spring-animations
contents.content: Good for

contents.heading: spring-animations
contents.content: `.smooth`

contents.heading: spring-animations
contents.content: No bounce

contents.heading: spring-animations
contents.content: Layout changes, sheets, large surfaces

contents.heading: spring-animations
contents.content: `.snappy`

contents.heading: spring-animations
contents.content: Small bounce, quick

contents.heading: spring-animations
contents.content: Selection, toggles, small controls

contents.heading: spring-animations
contents.content: `.bouncy`

contents.heading: spring-animations
contents.content: Visible bounce

contents.heading: spring-animations
contents.content: Playful confirmations, badges, icons

contents.heading: spring-animations
contents.content: Each takes `duration:` and `extraBounce:` if you need to tune it, for example `.snappy(duration: 0.3, extraBounce: 0.1)`.

contents.heading: why-springs-beat-easing-curves
contents.content: Easing curves like `.easeInOut` have a fixed duration and assume the motion starts at rest. Real interfaces get interrupted: the user taps again mid-animation, or drags something that is still settling. When a spring is retargeted, SwiftUI carries the current velocity into the new motion, so the object bends toward the new target instead of stopping and restarting. That continuity is most of what makes an iOS interface feel physical. Keep `.linear` for things that really are linear, like a progress fill tied to a clock.

contents.heading: transitions
contents.content: Animations change a view that stays on screen. **Transitions** describe how a view enters or leaves the hierarchy, usually inside an `if`. A transition only plays when the insertion or removal happens inside an animated transaction.

contents.heading: transitions
contents.content: `.combined(with:)` runs two transitions together.

contents.heading: transitions
contents.content: `.asymmetric(insertion:removal:)` uses different motion on the way in and out. Arrivals can be lively; departures should be quick and quiet.

contents.heading: transitions
contents.content: iOS 17 adds `.blurReplace`, which works well when one piece of content swaps for another in place. `.push(from:)` slides content in from an edge.

contents.heading: transitions
contents.content: If a transition does not play, check two things: the change happened inside `withAnimation` (or under an `.animation(_:value:)` on a parent), and the view really left the hierarchy rather than just changing opacity.

contents.heading: matchedgeometryeffect
contents.content: `matchedGeometryEffect` tells SwiftUI that two views in different places are the same thing, so it animates the frame from one to the other. The classic use is a selection indicator that glides between options.

contents.heading: matchedgeometryeffect
contents.content: Only one view with a given `id` should be visible at a time (or mark one as `isSource: false`). For morphing a card into a detail screen, the same idea applies across a larger hierarchy. Prompt Chips uses it to morph a tapped suggestion into a composer-width block.

contents.heading: phaseanimator-and-keyframeanimator
contents.content: Both are iOS 17 APIs for motion that has more than two states.

contents.heading: phaseanimator
contents.content: `phaseAnimator` steps through a sequence of values, animating between each one. Give it a `trigger` to run once per change, or leave the trigger out to loop forever.

contents.heading: keyframeanimator
contents.content: `keyframeAnimator` gives each property its own timeline. Use it when scale, offset, and rotation should not move in lockstep.

contents.heading: keyframeanimator
contents.content: The press-in, pop, and settle pattern here is the same shape Reaction Toggle builds on, with a color flood and a halo on top.

contents.heading: animating-numbers-and-text
contents.content: `contentTransition(.numericText(value:))` rolls digits instead of cross-fading the whole label. Add `.monospacedDigit()` so the width does not jump.

contents.heading: animating-numbers-and-text
contents.content: Passing `value:` tells SwiftUI the direction, so digits roll up when the number grows and down when it shrinks. For a mechanical counter where each digit rolls on its own slot and carries from the low digits up, see Odometer. For headlines that rise in by character, word, or line with a stagger, see Text Reveal.

contents.heading: scrolltransition
contents.content: `scrollTransition` gives each child a `phase` as it enters, sits in, and leaves the visible area. `phase.value` runs from -1 (leading edge) through 0 (fully visible) to 1 (trailing edge).

contents.heading: scrolltransition
contents.content: Depth Carousel takes this further: pages recede in depth away from center, each page gets a phase value for inner parallax, and the page indicator is computed in absolute page coordinates so it never jumps.

contents.heading: visualeffect
contents.content: `visualEffect` hands you a `GeometryProxy` without affecting layout, so you can drive effects from a view's position cheaply.

contents.heading: visualeffect
contents.content: This replaces the old pattern of reading a `GeometryReader` into `@State` on every scroll frame, which re-evaluates your view body far more than it needs to.

contents.heading: gesture-driven-motion-that-keeps-velocity
contents.content: The difference between a drag that feels native and one that feels cheap is what happens on release. A good release decides based on where the finger was *heading* (`predictedEndTranslation`) and hands the finger's velocity to the spring, so there is no speed jump at the moment you let go.

contents.heading: gesture-driven-motion-that-keeps-velocity
contents.content: Two details matter here:

contents.heading: gesture-driven-motion-that-keeps-velocity
contents.content: **Decide on the projection, not the position.** A short, fast flick should throw the card even though the finger only moved 60 points. `predictedEndTranslation` captures that.

contents.heading: gesture-driven-motion-that-keeps-velocity
contents.content: **Normalize the velocity.** `initialVelocity` is measured in "distances per second", where 1 means the full distance to the target. Dividing points per second by the remaining distance gets you there.

contents.heading: gesture-driven-motion-that-keeps-velocity
contents.content: This is the core of Swipe Deck, which adds an outcome badge that locks at the threshold and cards beneath that rise as the top one leaves. Drag to Dismiss applies it to photos and sheets on two axes, and Flip Card uses a drag to scrub a 3D rotation, then commits or snaps back by velocity.

contents.heading: respect-reduce-motion
contents.content: Some people get motion sick from large movement, parallax, and zooms. Read `accessibilityReduceMotion` and swap spatial motion for a short fade. Do not remove feedback entirely: state changes still need to be visible.

contents.heading: respect-reduce-motion
contents.content: What to reduce: travel across the screen, parallax, 3D rotation, zooming, looping motion. What to keep: opacity changes, color changes, and small scale feedback on press. Every SwiftPieces component reads this setting. Elastic Button, for example, keeps its scale and darken under Reduce Motion but drops the lean and stretch toward the finger.

contents.heading: performance-notes
contents.content: **Prefer render effects over layout.** `scaleEffect`, `offset`, `opacity`, and `rotationEffect` do not trigger layout. Animating `frame` or padding on hundreds of views does.

contents.heading: performance-notes
contents.content: **Scope animations tightly.** `.animation(_:value:)` on the smallest view that needs it, or the iOS 17 `.animation(_:body:)` form, avoids animating unrelated changes.

contents.heading: performance-notes
contents.content: **Use `visualEffect` and `scrollTransition` instead of geometry in state.** Writing scroll offsets into `@State` every frame re-runs bodies for no visible gain.

contents.heading: performance-notes
contents.content: **Flatten complex drawings.** `drawingGroup()` renders a subtree into one layer, which helps with many overlapping shapes and gradients. Test it, since it can hurt simple views.

contents.heading: performance-notes
contents.content: **Stabilize identity.** Views in a `ForEach` need stable ids, or SwiftUI treats a moved row as a removal plus an insertion and plays transitions you did not ask for.

contents.heading: performance-notes
contents.content: **Measure on a device.** The simulator hides frame drops. Profile with Instruments on real hardware, ideally a slower one.

title: SwiftUI Buttons: Custom Styles, Animation, Loading
description: SwiftUI buttons from the basics to custom ButtonStyle, press animation, haptics, async loading states, hold to confirm, and accessible hit targets.

contents.content: A SwiftUI button is a `Button` view: an action closure plus a label, styled separately through `ButtonStyle`. Keep the action and label in the `Button`, and put the look and the press animation in a style you can reuse across the app.

This guide goes from roles and built-in styles to a custom press-scale style with a spring, haptics, an async loading button with success and error states, hold to confirm for destructive actions, and the accessibility details that are easy to miss. Every snippet compiles against the iOS 17 SDK.

contents.heading: button-basics-and-roles
contents.content: A **role** describes what the button does, not how it looks. `.destructive` tints the label red in system styles, and in alerts, confirmation dialogs, and swipe actions it also changes placement. `.cancel` tells the system which button dismisses. Always set roles, because system containers rely on them and VoiceOver users benefit from the ordering they produce.

contents.heading: button-basics-and-roles
contents.content: Prefer the `Label` or `systemImage:` forms over hand-built `HStack`s. The label adapts to its context (icon only in toolbars, title and icon in menus) and reads correctly to VoiceOver.

contents.heading: built-in-button-styles
contents.content: `.borderedProminent` is the filled primary action. Use one per screen.

contents.heading: built-in-button-styles
contents.content: `.bordered` is a tinted secondary action.

contents.heading: built-in-button-styles
contents.content: `.controlSize` and `.buttonBorderShape` adjust size and shape without a custom style.

contents.heading: built-in-button-styles
contents.content: `.glass` and `.glassProminent` are **iOS 26 only** and render Liquid Glass. Gate them with `#available` if you support iOS 17. The Liquid Glass docs cover fallbacks.

contents.heading: buttonstyle-vs-primitivebuttonstyle
contents.content: Both let you restyle any `Button` with `.buttonStyle(_:)`. The difference is who owns the interaction.

contents.heading: buttonstyle-vs-primitivebuttonstyle
contents.content: **`ButtonStyle`** keeps the system's tap handling. You get `configuration.label`, `configuration.role`, and `configuration.isPressed`, and you only decide how the button looks in each state. This is what you want almost every time.

contents.heading: buttonstyle-vs-primitivebuttonstyle
contents.content: **`PrimitiveButtonStyle`** hands you `configuration.trigger()` and makes you define the gesture yourself. Use it when the activation itself changes, for example a button that fires on a long press:

contents.heading: buttonstyle-vs-primitivebuttonstyle
contents.content: With a primitive style you lose the system's pressed state, cancellation when the finger slides off, and some accessibility behavior, so you rebuild those yourself.

contents.heading: a-custom-button-style-with-a-spring-press
contents.content: A good press style does three things: it responds instantly on touch down, it springs back on release, and it still looks disabled when the button is disabled.

contents.heading: a-custom-button-style-with-a-spring-press
contents.content: Use it like a system style: `Button("Continue") { }.buttonStyle(.pressScale)`.

contents.heading: a-custom-button-style-with-a-spring-press
contents.content: The two springs are the important part. Pressing in uses a short, unbouncy spring so the button reacts under the finger with no lag. Releasing uses a longer spring with bounce, so it settles with a little life. One spring for both directions either feels sluggish on press or twitchy on release.

contents.heading: a-custom-button-style-with-a-spring-press
contents.content: This is the simple version. Elastic Button is the full one: a `ButtonStyle` that squashes toward the touch point, stretches with rubber-band resistance when dragged, deepens after a hold, and snaps back with a spring. You apply it the same way:

contents.heading: haptics-on-press
contents.content: `sensoryFeedback` (iOS 17) plays a haptic when a value changes. Attach it to the button and trigger it from the action:

contents.heading: haptics-on-press
contents.content: For feedback on touch down rather than on release, trigger from `isPressed` inside the style and return `nil` when you want silence:

contents.heading: haptics-on-press
contents.content: Keep press haptics light and reserve `.success`, `.warning`, and `.error` for outcomes. The SwiftUI haptics guide goes deeper.

contents.heading: a-loading-button-with-success-and-error-states
contents.content: Async buttons are where most apps feel unfinished: a spinner appears, nothing tells you it worked, and a double tap sends the request twice. Model the button as a small state machine instead of a pile of booleans.

contents.heading: a-loading-button-with-success-and-error-states
contents.content: What this gets right:

contents.heading: a-loading-button-with-success-and-error-states
contents.content: **One source of truth.** The label, disabled state, haptic, and VoiceOver text all derive from `phase`.

contents.heading: a-loading-button-with-success-and-error-states
contents.content: **No double submits.** The button is disabled while loading, and `run()` guards against re-entry.

contents.heading: a-loading-button-with-success-and-error-states
contents.content: **Success is visible.** The check holds for a moment before returning to idle.

contents.heading: a-loading-button-with-success-and-error-states
contents.content: **Errors are recoverable.** The failed state becomes the retry, with the message shown below.

contents.heading: a-loading-button-with-success-and-error-states
contents.content: Commit Button is the designed version of this state machine. It uses one idle, loading, success, error, and disabled phase: the capsule collapses to a spinning ring, blooms into a success block with a drawn check, or re-expands as an error block that shakes and doubles as retry. Its API mirrors the pattern above:

contents.heading: a-loading-button-with-success-and-error-states
contents.content: For whole-screen results after an action, see the loading states guide.

contents.heading: hold-to-confirm-for-destructive-actions
contents.content: A confirmation alert interrupts every user to protect the few who tapped by mistake. For deletes, transfers, and other irreversible actions, a press-and-hold button is often better: it is fast when intended and nearly impossible to trigger by accident.

contents.heading: hold-to-confirm-for-destructive-actions
contents.content: The fill runs on a linear animation because it represents time, and it rewinds with a spring on early release so the user sees the action was cancelled. Hold to Confirm adds milestone dots with rising haptics along the way, inverts the label as the fill passes under it, and settles into a confirmed block:

contents.heading: hit-targets
contents.content: Apple's Human Interface Guidelines ask for touch targets of at least 44 by 44 points. Icon buttons are the usual offenders, because a 17-point glyph produces a 17-point target.

contents.heading: hit-targets
contents.content: `contentShape` makes the whole frame tappable, including transparent areas. Small toggles like a like or save button need the same treatment. Reaction Toggle is a good reference for a compact control that still presses in, floods with color, and sends out a halo on toggle.

contents.heading: common-button-mistakes
contents.content: **Using `onTapGesture` instead of `Button`.** A tap gesture on a view gives you no pressed state, no disabled state, no keyboard or Switch Control support, and no button trait for VoiceOver. If it performs an action, make it a `Button` and style it.

contents.heading: common-button-mistakes
contents.content: **Styling inside the label.** Padding, backgrounds, and press effects written directly into the label have to be copied to every button. Move them into a `ButtonStyle` once, and the whole app stays consistent when you change it.

contents.heading: common-button-mistakes
contents.content: **Animating the press with `withAnimation` in the action.** The action runs on release, so the button looks dead while the finger is down. Press feedback belongs in the style, driven by `configuration.isPressed`, which updates on touch down.

contents.heading: common-button-mistakes
contents.content: **Forgetting the cancel path.** Users often start a press, change their mind, and slide off. `ButtonStyle` handles this for free: `isPressed` goes false and the action never fires. Custom gestures in a `PrimitiveButtonStyle` or on a plain view have to handle it themselves.

contents.heading: common-button-mistakes
contents.content: **Hiding a failure.** A loading button that silently returns to idle after an error is worse than no loading state at all. Show the error next to the button and make the next tap a retry.

contents.heading: common-button-mistakes
contents.content: **One animation for everything.** A primary action, a destructive action, and a small toggle deserve different weights. Give the primary action the fuller press, keep secondary buttons quieter, and let only confirmations bounce.

contents.heading: accessibility-checklist
contents.content: **Labels.** Icon-only buttons need `.accessibilityLabel`. Use a verb or a clear noun: "Close", "Share photo", not "X".

contents.heading: accessibility-checklist
contents.content: **State.** Loading and success states should change the label or value so VoiceOver users know what happened.

contents.heading: accessibility-checklist
contents.content: **Dynamic Type.** Use `minHeight` rather than a fixed `height`, and let text wrap. For custom sizes, `@ScaledMetric` scales padding and icon sizes with the user's text size.

contents.heading: accessibility-checklist
contents.content: **Reduce Motion.** Keep pressed feedback (opacity, color, a small scale) but drop travel, stretch, and bounce. The `PressScaleStyle` above does this.

contents.heading: accessibility-checklist
contents.content: **Disabled is a design state.** Read `@Environment(\.isEnabled)` in custom styles and draw a distinct disabled look instead of relying on opacity alone.

contents.heading: accessibility-checklist
contents.content: **Destructive actions.** Set `role: .destructive`, and for hold gestures make sure the VoiceOver path is clear.

contents.heading: menus-that-grow-from-a-button
contents.content: When one button needs to expose several actions, reach for `Menu` first. For a floating action button that fans out, Glass Action Menu long-presses open into a line or arc of actions you can slide across and release to fire, and its glass morphs on iOS 26.

title: SwiftUI Cards: Card Views, Swipe Stacks and Flip Cards
description: Build SwiftUI cards that feel native: continuous corners, layered shadows, press states, a swipeable card stack, a 3D flip card, tilt and scroll parallax.

contents.content: A SwiftUI card is a view with a rounded, continuous-corner background, a soft shadow that separates it from the surface, and usually one interaction: tap, press, swipe or flip. There is no built-in `Card` type. You compose it from a shape, a background and modifiers, which means the quality is entirely in the details.

This guide builds the common card patterns from scratch: a basic card, a pressable card, a Tinder-style swipe stack, a 3D flip card, a device-tilt card, and parallax in a scroll view. Everything targets iOS 17.

contents.heading: a-basic-card-view
contents.content: Three details separate a card that looks native from one that looks like a web port: continuous corners, a layered shadow, and a hairline edge.

contents.heading: a-basic-card-view
contents.content: **Continuous corners.** `style: .continuous` gives the squircle curve Apple uses for app icons and system sheets. The default circular style has a visible kink where the straight edge meets the arc. On a large card you can see it.

contents.heading: a-basic-card-view
contents.content: **Layered shadows.** One big blurry shadow looks like a glow. Real objects cast a tight contact shadow plus a wide ambient one. Stacking two `.shadow` modifiers, a small radius with low offset and a large radius with a larger offset, reads as depth without haze.

contents.heading: a-basic-card-view
contents.content: **Hairline edge.** In dark mode shadows nearly vanish. A `strokeBorder` at very low opacity keeps the card's edge visible on any background. `strokeBorder` insets the stroke, so it never spills outside the shape.

contents.heading: a-basic-card-view
contents.content: Apply `.shadow` after `.background`, and make sure the background is opaque. A shadow on a translucent view is cast by every child, text included.

contents.heading: a-tappable-pressable-card
contents.content: Wrap the card in a `Button` so it gets accessibility traits, keyboard support and correct hit testing for free. Then give it a press state with a custom `ButtonStyle`.

contents.heading: a-tappable-pressable-card
contents.content: Keep the scale small. At 0.97 a full-width card visibly responds; at 0.9 it looks like it is falling away. The SwiftUI buttons guide covers press states in more depth.

contents.heading: a-swipeable-card-stack
contents.content: The swipe stack has four parts: a `ZStack` of cards, a `DragGesture` on the top card only, a rotation that swings from the bottom edge, and a release rule that decides between throwing the card and snapping it back.

contents.heading: a-swipeable-card-stack
contents.content: The details that matter:

contents.heading: a-swipeable-card-stack
contents.content: **The top card is the last element.** In a `ZStack` later views draw on top, so `removeLast()` removes the visible card.

contents.heading: a-swipeable-card-stack
contents.content: **Rotate from `.bottom`.** Rotating around the center makes the card spin in place. Anchoring at the bottom makes it swing like something held at its base, which is how a hand moves it.

contents.heading: a-swipeable-card-stack
contents.content: **Use `predictedEndTranslation`, not `translation`.** It includes the gesture's velocity, so a short fast flick counts as a swipe while a slow drag that stops short springs back. This is the single biggest difference between a stack that feels right and one that feels sticky.

contents.heading: a-swipeable-card-stack
contents.content: **Remove after the throw.** `withAnimation(_:completion:)` (iOS 17) lets the card finish leaving the screen before it is removed from the array.

contents.heading: a-swipeable-card-stack
contents.content: Production stacks need more: a badge that fades in with drag progress and locks at the threshold, the next card rising as the top one leaves, an up-swipe, a haptic at the threshold, and a way to trigger swipes from buttons. Swipe Deck does all of that, including a threshold tick through `sensoryFeedback`. The SwiftUI haptics guide explains that pattern.

contents.heading: accessibility-for-swipes
contents.content: A swipe is invisible to VoiceOver. Every direction must also exist as a named action, which is what the `accessibilityAction(named:)` lines above do. VoiceOver users reach them through the actions rotor. Without them, the stack is unusable for anyone who cannot perform the gesture.

contents.heading: a-3d-flip-card
contents.content: A flip card rotates around the y axis with `rotation3DEffect`. Two problems catch everyone the first time: the back face renders mirrored, and both faces show during the turn.

contents.heading: a-3d-flip-card
contents.content: The fix for the mirror is to pre-rotate the back face 180 degrees, so the container's rotation cancels it out. The fix for the overlap is to choose the visible face from the current angle, on every frame of the animation. A view that conforms to `Animatable` gets exactly that.

contents.heading: a-3d-flip-card
contents.content: If you animated `opacity` directly with `isFlipped`, SwiftUI would cross-fade the faces over the whole turn, and at 90 degrees you would see half of each. Because `FlipFaces` is `Animatable`, its `body` runs with the interpolated angle, and the swap happens exactly when the card is edge-on. The `perspective` value controls how strong the depth looks; lower values flatten it.

contents.heading: a-3d-flip-card
contents.content: In a real app, replace the fixed accessibility label with a description of the visible face's content. Flip Card goes further: you can drag sideways to scrub the rotation, release commits or snaps back by velocity, the card lifts toward you mid-turn, and each face shades as it turns edge-on.

contents.heading: device-tilt-cards-with-core-motion
contents.content: A card that tilts as you tilt the phone uses `CMMotionManager` device motion. Two rules matter more than the visual: filter the signal, and stop updates whenever the card is not on screen or the app is not active. Motion updates run the sensors continuously and cost battery.

contents.heading: device-tilt-cards-with-core-motion
contents.content: Attitude values are in radians, so a small multiplier gives a few degrees of tilt. Relative attitude matters: without the reference, a phone held upright reads as a large pitch and the card sits permanently tipped back.

contents.heading: device-tilt-cards-with-core-motion
contents.content: Stop motion updates in `onDisappear` and when `scenePhase` leaves `.active`. A card in a scrolled-away tab that keeps the sensors running is a quiet battery drain that is hard to trace later. Under Reduce Motion, do not start updates at all.

contents.heading: device-tilt-cards-with-core-motion
contents.content: Motion Card follows these rules: an exponential filter, a fixed-light sheen and layered shadow that slide as it turns, a press that settles it flat with a light impact, and Core Motion that stops whenever the scene is not active.

contents.heading: parallax-cards-in-a-scroll-view
contents.content: iOS 17 added `visualEffect`, which gives you a `GeometryProxy` for a view without a `GeometryReader` changing its layout. Read the view's frame in the `.scrollView` coordinate space and offset the inner content by a fraction of it.

contents.heading: parallax-cards-in-a-scroll-view
contents.content: With a photo instead of a symbol, make the image taller than the card by the maximum drift, so its edges never show through. Parallax Card oversizes the image that way and moves a caption block at a slower rate still, so the card reads in three layers.

contents.heading: parallax-cards-in-a-scroll-view
contents.content: For horizontal carousels, `scrollTransition` is simpler. It hands you a phase (`-1` leaving on one side, `0` centered, `1` on the other) and lets you scale, fade or rotate each card from it.

contents.heading: parallax-cards-in-a-scroll-view
contents.content: Depth Carousel builds on this idea: paged cards recede in depth as they leave center, each page gets a phase value for its own inner parallax, and a scrubbable pill indicator tracks the page position.

contents.heading: accessibility-checklist-for-cards
contents.content: Tappable cards are `Button`s, or at least carry `.isButton` and an action.

contents.heading: accessibility-checklist-for-cards
contents.content: Every gesture (swipe, flip, drag) has an `accessibilityAction` equivalent.

contents.heading: accessibility-checklist-for-cards
contents.content: Card content reads as one element where it makes sense (`.accessibilityElement(children: .combine)`), so VoiceOver does not stop on every label.

contents.heading: accessibility-checklist-for-cards
contents.content: Tilt, parallax and 3D rotation are reduced or removed under Reduce Motion.

contents.heading: accessibility-checklist-for-cards
contents.content: Text on image cards sits on an opaque block or a scrim with enough contrast.

title: SwiftUI Haptics: sensoryFeedback and Haptic Feedback
description: A practical guide to SwiftUI haptics: sensoryFeedback triggers, conditions and feedback kinds, drag threshold ticks, UIKit generators, and restraint.

contents.content: SwiftUI haptics are declarative: you attach `.sensoryFeedback(_:trigger:)` to a view, and SwiftUI plays the feedback every time the trigger value changes. It shipped in iOS 17, and in SwiftUI code it replaces most uses of `UIImpactFeedbackGenerator` in SwiftUI code because there is no generator to create, prepare or keep alive.

The API is small. The hard part is taste: picking the right kind, firing it at the exact moment an animation crosses a meaningful line, and staying quiet the rest of the time. This guide covers all three.

contents.heading: the-basic-modifier
contents.content: `sensoryFeedback` watches an `Equatable` value. When the value changes, the feedback plays. You do not call anything imperatively, you change state.

contents.heading: the-basic-modifier
contents.content: A counter is the most reliable trigger for one-shot events. A `Bool` works too, but it only fires when it flips, so setting `true` twice in a row plays once. If you want a haptic every time an event happens, increment an `Int`.

contents.heading: three-variants-of-sensoryfeedback
contents.content: There are three overloads, and each solves a different problem.

contents.heading: 1-fixed-feedback
contents.content: `.sensoryFeedback(.selection, trigger: value)` plays the same feedback on every change. Use it when every change means the same thing.

contents.heading: 2-condition-closure
contents.content: Pass a closure that receives the old and new values and returns `Bool`. The feedback plays only when it returns `true`. This lets you stack two modifiers on one trigger: a light tick for ordinary steps and a firmer bump at the bounds.

contents.heading: 3-feedback-returning-closure
contents.content: The third form drops the first argument. The closure returns a `SensoryFeedback?`, so it can choose the kind per change, or return `nil` to stay silent.

contents.heading: 3-feedback-returning-closure
contents.content: Scrub Stepper uses exactly this shape: a selection tick while you scrub across the numeral, `.increase` or `.decrease` on taps, and a separate rigid impact at the bounds.

contents.heading: the-feedback-kinds
contents.content: `SensoryFeedback` has a fixed set of cases. They are semantic, so pick by meaning, not by how strong you want it to feel.

contents.heading: the-feedback-kinds
contents.content: Kind

contents.heading: the-feedback-kinds
contents.content: Use it for

contents.heading: the-feedback-kinds
contents.content: `.selection`

contents.heading: the-feedback-kinds
contents.content: A value moved one step: picker rows, slider steps, scrubbing across items. The lightest tick.

contents.heading: the-feedback-kinds
contents.content: `.impact(weight:intensity:)`

contents.heading: the-feedback-kinds
contents.content: A physical collision. Weight is `.light`, `.medium` or `.heavy`, intensity is 0 to 1.

contents.heading: the-feedback-kinds
contents.content: `.impact(flexibility:intensity:)`

contents.heading: the-feedback-kinds
contents.content: The same, described by material: `.rigid`, `.solid` or `.soft`. Rigid feels like a hard detent, soft like a cushion.

contents.heading: the-feedback-kinds
contents.content: `.success`, `.warning`, `.error`

contents.heading: the-feedback-kinds
contents.content: The outcome of a task. Reserve these for results, not for taps.

contents.heading: the-feedback-kinds
contents.content: `.increase`, `.decrease`

contents.heading: the-feedback-kinds
contents.content: A value went up or down, such as a stepper.

contents.heading: the-feedback-kinds
contents.content: `.alignment`

contents.heading: the-feedback-kinds
contents.content: Something snapped into alignment, such as a dragged item meeting a guide.

contents.heading: the-feedback-kinds
contents.content: `.levelChange`

contents.heading: the-feedback-kinds
contents.content: Moved between discrete levels, like pressure stages.

contents.heading: the-feedback-kinds
contents.content: `.start`, `.stop`

contents.heading: the-feedback-kinds
contents.content: An activity began or ended, such as a recording or timer.

contents.heading: the-feedback-kinds
contents.content: Plain `.impact` with no arguments also exists. The actual pattern each kind plays is up to the system and the hardware, and some kinds (`.alignment`, `.levelChange`, `.start`, `.stop`) were designed with other Apple platforms in mind, so test on a real iPhone before relying on one to feel distinct. The Simulator plays nothing.

contents.heading: a-quick-decision-guide
contents.content: The user is **choosing** among values: `.selection`.

contents.heading: a-quick-decision-guide
contents.content: Something **hit a wall** or **locked into place**: `.impact`, rigid or heavy.

contents.heading: a-quick-decision-guide
contents.content: Something **committed**: a single `.impact` at the moment of commit, then `.success` when the work actually finishes.

contents.heading: a-quick-decision-guide
contents.content: Something **failed**: `.error`, once, alongside a visible error state.

contents.heading: haptics-at-animation-thresholds
contents.content: The best haptics mark a moment the eye is already watching: a card crossing the point where release will throw it, a knob landing on a detent, a hold reaching its end. The pattern is always the same. Derive a discrete value from continuous gesture state, and put the haptic on the discrete value.

contents.heading: tick-when-a-drag-crosses-a-threshold
contents.content: Drag offset changes every frame, so it is a terrible trigger. A `Bool` that says "past the threshold" changes twice per gesture at most.

contents.heading: tick-when-a-drag-crosses-a-threshold
contents.content: The condition closure plays the impact only when the row arms, not when it disarms. The color change and the haptic land on the same frame, which is what makes it feel physical. Swipe Deck does the same thing with a computed boolean, `lift >= 1`, so the tick fires when the outcome badge locks at the threshold, and a solid impact fires when the card is actually thrown.

contents.heading: detents-on-a-continuous-control
contents.content: For dials and sliders, quantize the value into steps and tick on each step, with a heavier bump on major marks.

contents.heading: detents-on-a-continuous-control
contents.content: This is the structure behind Timer Dial: a selection tick per step, a rigid impact every 5 seconds, and `.success` when the countdown finishes. Range Slider ticks every step and switches to a firmer impact when a thumb hits a bound or the minimum gap. Rating Scrub ticks between stars and uses a rigid impact at zero and at the maximum.

contents.heading: escalating-feedback-over-time
contents.content: Hold interactions benefit from feedback that builds. Hold to Confirm passes three milestone dots while you hold, each with a soft impact of rising intensity, then plays `.success` on commit. The rising intensity tells the user "keep going" without any text. Fan Stack uses the other end of the range: a soft impact as the avatars fan out, a selection tick each time your finger crosses a new face, and a solid impact on select.

contents.heading: escalating-feedback-over-time
contents.content: Keep the haptic and the visual on the same state change. If the haptic fires from `onChanged` but the animation runs from a separate timer, they drift apart by a frame or two and the interaction feels loose.

contents.heading: uikit-feedback-generators
contents.content: `sensoryFeedback` needs iOS 17. For older targets, or for code outside a view (a view model, a game loop, a UIKit controller), use the generators directly.

contents.heading: uikit-feedback-generators
contents.content: There are three generator classes: `UIImpactFeedbackGenerator` (styles `.light`, `.medium`, `.heavy`, `.soft`, `.rigid`, plus `impactOccurred(intensity:)`), `UISelectionFeedbackGenerator`, and `UINotificationFeedbackGenerator` (`.success`, `.warning`, `.error`). Call `prepare()` shortly before you expect to fire, for example when a drag begins, so the Taptic Engine is awake and the first tick is not late.

contents.heading: uikit-feedback-generators
contents.content: In SwiftUI on iOS 17 and later, prefer the modifier. It ties feedback to state, which keeps it in sync with animations and makes it easy to test by reading the state.

contents.heading: core-haptics-briefly
contents.content: Core Haptics (`CHHapticEngine`) is for custom patterns: a textured rumble, a heartbeat, a sequence synced to audio. You describe events with intensity and sharpness and play them through an engine you keep alive.

contents.heading: core-haptics-briefly
contents.content: Keep the engine as a stored property. A local engine is released when the function returns and the pattern stops. For production use you also handle `stoppedHandler` and `resetHandler` to restart the engine after an interruption. Most interface work never needs Core Haptics. Reach for it only when none of the semantic kinds say what you mean.

contents.heading: restraint-and-accessibility
contents.content: Haptics are a shared, physical channel. Overuse numbs people to the ones that matter.

contents.heading: restraint-and-accessibility
contents.content: **One haptic per meaningful moment.** Not on every tap of a normal button (the system already gives feedback where it should), not on scroll, not on appear.

contents.heading: restraint-and-accessibility
contents.content: **Never tie a haptic to a per-frame value.** Quantize first, as in the detent example.

contents.heading: restraint-and-accessibility
contents.content: **Match intensity to consequence.** A selection tick for browsing, an impact for committing, a notification kind for results.

contents.heading: restraint-and-accessibility
contents.content: **Pair every haptic with a visual.** Some devices have no Taptic Engine, and some people turn System Haptics off in Settings. The haptic confirms, it never carries information alone.

contents.heading: restraint-and-accessibility
contents.content: **Respect the rest of the system.** Under Reduce Motion, a threshold still deserves its tick, but the animation around it should shorten. Haptics are often more important for VoiceOver users, so actions exposed through `accessibilityAction` or `accessibilityAdjustableAction` should play the same feedback as the gesture path.

contents.heading: restraint-and-accessibility
contents.content: The system switch is handled for you: `sensoryFeedback` and the UIKit generators stay silent when the user has disabled System Haptics.

contents.heading: where-the-hard-version-already-exists
contents.content: The patterns above cover most apps. The hard part is tuning, and every piece in the haptics hub ships with it done: thresholds that match the visuals, bound impacts that differ from step ticks, and escalation that reads as progress. If you are also working on the motion side, SwiftUI animations covers springs and phase animators, and SwiftUI buttons covers press states that pair with a tap haptic.

title: SwiftUI Skeleton Loading, Shimmer and Loading States
description: SwiftUI skeleton loading with redacted placeholders, a shimmer modifier, ProgressView styles, success and failure morphs, paging footers and Reduce Motion.

contents.content: SwiftUI skeleton loading uses `.redacted(reason: .placeholder)` to draw your real layout as gray shapes while data loads, then swaps in content when it arrives. Add a shimmer (a soft highlight sweeping across the shapes) and the screen reads as "loading" without a spinner, and without the layout jumping when content lands.

Skeletons are one loading state among several. This guide covers the skeleton itself, a shimmer you can reuse, `ProgressView`, the handoff from placeholder to content, an action that morphs through loading, success and failure, infinite-scroll footers, and an AI "thinking" placeholder. Everything targets iOS 17 and respects Reduce Motion.

contents.heading: skeletons-with-redactedreason
contents.content: `redacted(reason: .placeholder)` replaces text with rounded bars the size of the text, and tints images and shapes. You feed it placeholder data of a realistic length, so the skeleton has the same shape as the loaded screen.

contents.heading: skeletons-with-redactedreason
contents.content: `unredacted()` opts a subview out. Use it for chrome that does not depend on data: an icon, a section label, a button. Keeping those visible makes the skeleton feel like the real screen arriving rather than a generic gray block.

contents.heading: skeletons-with-redactedreason
contents.content: Two things to know:

contents.heading: skeletons-with-redactedreason
contents.content: **Redaction is an environment value.** Custom views can read `@Environment(\.redactionReasons)` and draw their own placeholder, for example hiding a chart that would otherwise render with fake numbers.

contents.heading: skeletons-with-redactedreason
contents.content: **Placeholder text length is the layout.** A one-word placeholder title makes a short bar, and the row jumps when a two-line headline arrives. Pick placeholder strings that match typical content.

contents.heading: a-shimmer-modifier
contents.content: A shimmer is a light gradient that moves across the placeholder, masked to its shapes. The simplest version animates an offset with `repeatForever`.

contents.heading: a-shimmer-modifier
contents.content: `.mask(content)` is the key line. The gradient only paints where the redacted content has pixels, so it sweeps across the bars and blocks, never across the gaps.

contents.heading: a-clock-driven-shimmer-with-timelineview
contents.content: `repeatForever` has a weakness: every row starts its own animation when it appears, so rows that scroll in later are out of phase with the rest. Driving the shimmer from `TimelineView` puts every instance on the same wall clock, and it can be switched off cleanly.

contents.heading: a-clock-driven-shimmer-with-timelineview
contents.content: Because the phase comes from the date, not from per-view state, ten rows read as one surface with one highlight passing over it. Skeleton Loader uses the same idea: a self-masking modifier that turns any layout, color blocks included, into one quiet shape sweeping a diagonal highlight on a shared clock.

contents.heading: progressview-styles
contents.content: Skeletons suit content. For actions and unknown waits in small spaces, `ProgressView` is still the right tool.

contents.heading: progressview-styles
contents.content: A `ProgressView` without a value is indeterminate. With `value:` it is determinate, and `fractionCompleted` in a custom style is non-nil. On iOS, `.circular` with a value still draws the indeterminate spinner, so a determinate ring needs a custom `ProgressViewStyle` like the one above.

contents.heading: progressview-styles
contents.content: A rough rule: under about a second, show nothing. For a known layout, show a skeleton. For an action the user started, show progress on the control they touched. For a long task with a known size, show a determinate bar.

contents.heading: handing-off-from-skeleton-to-content
contents.content: The handoff is where most loading states feel cheap: gray bars vanish and content pops in. Keep the same view, flip the redaction, and animate the change.

contents.heading: handing-off-from-skeleton-to-content
contents.content: Because the view identity never changes, the layout does not jump. For lists, stagger the reveal by index so rows settle top to bottom. Skeleton Loader hands off this way: content unblurs and rises row by row, and its `.skeleton(isLoading:staggerIndex:)` modifier takes the row index to compute the delay. It also takes an `isFailed` flag for the case where loading ends in an error.

contents.heading: loading-success-and-failure-in-one-control
contents.content: When the user starts an action, the button they tapped should become the loading state, then the result. Model it as one phase enum rather than a pile of booleans.

contents.heading: loading-success-and-failure-in-one-control
contents.content: `contentTransition(.symbolEffect(.replace))` animates the symbol swap, and the failure state doubles as retry. Haptics fire on the result, not on the tap; the SwiftUI haptics guide explains why.

contents.heading: loading-success-and-failure-in-one-control
contents.content: The polished versions of this pattern are a single continuous shape rather than swapped icons. Status Morph is one stroke that spins as a loading arc, closes into a ring, floods into a solid block and draws a check on success, or a cross with a nudge on failure. Commit Button applies the same idea to a button driven by one idle, loading, success, error and disabled phase, where the error state shakes and doubles as retry. When the result deserves a full screen, Outcome Screen covers success, failure and empty outcomes with async retry.

contents.heading: infinite-scroll-footer-states
contents.content: A paged list has four footer states, and each needs a distinct view: idle (nothing), loading (a spinner), failed (a message and a retry that keeps loaded rows), and end (a quiet "all caught up").

contents.heading: infinite-scroll-footer-states
contents.content: The guard on `footer == .idle` prevents two loads at once, loading starts five rows before the end so the spinner is rarely seen, and duplicate ids are dropped when pages overlap. What this sketch leaves out is refresh: a response that arrives after a pull to refresh must be ignored, not appended. Paged List handles that, along with skeleton rows for the first page and pull to refresh that replaces rows only on success.

contents.heading: an-ai-thinking-placeholder
contents.content: A chat reply that has not started streaming needs a placeholder too. Three dots on a shared clock are the classic version.

contents.heading: an-ai-thinking-placeholder
contents.content: A better placeholder is shaped like the reply it becomes, so the answer replaces it without a jump. Thinking State offers three presentations on one clock (rising dots, a sheen over reply-shaped bars, or a label whose glyphs carry the sheen), an elapsed-seconds label, and a `.thinkingState()` modifier that sweeps any view.

contents.heading: reduce-motion
contents.content: Loading animations loop, which makes them the most tiring motion on screen for people sensitive to it. Every example above reads `accessibilityReduceMotion`:

contents.heading: reduce-motion
contents.content: **Shimmer:** drop the sweep entirely. The static redacted shapes still say "loading".

contents.heading: reduce-motion
contents.content: **Spinners and dots:** pause the clock (`TimelineView(.animation(paused:))`) or show a static state.

contents.heading: reduce-motion
contents.content: **Pulses:** replace with a fixed mid opacity.

contents.heading: reduce-motion
contents.content: **Handoffs:** swap blur-and-rise for a short cross-fade.

contents.heading: reduce-motion
contents.content: **Result morphs:** keep the color and symbol change, drop the shake.

contents.heading: reduce-motion
contents.content: Reduce Motion does not mean no feedback. It means the state still changes clearly, just without looping or travelling motion.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Assistant replies sit on the ground under a header: a 24pt ink mark, the name (`style.assistantName`) and a small uppercase phase label (THINKING, WRITING, STOPPED). User prompts are a solid block (`style.userBlock`, sky) with dark ink and a tucked bottom-trailing corner. Set `style.showsHeader = false` for a bare reply.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Text is split into word tokens (each word keeps its trailing whitespace). On iOS 18 a private `TextRenderer` draws each token at its own fade-in opacity with a 2pt rise; on iOS 17 the same opacities are written into the `AttributedString` runs. Only words that arrive after the view appears animate, so loaded history renders instantly.

contents.heading: notes

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The cursor is an inline tangerine capsule sized from the body font's cap height, so it flows with the text and scales with Dynamic Type. On iOS 18 it pulses through the renderer; on iOS 17 it is solid.

contents.content: Interactive dot grid. Resting dots are a tonal ramp on `Style.dot` (`.primary` by default, so both color schemes work); under the finger they swell and take on `Style.highlight`, a solid house block.

title: Flip Card
description: A two-sided card you flip by tap or by dragging sideways. The drag scrubs the rotation, release commits or snaps back by velocity, the card lifts toward you mid-turn with a layered shadow that slides off the raised edge, and each face shades as it turns edge-on.

contents.content: Two-sided card with tap-to-flip and drag-to-flip.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: One `DragGesture(minimumDistance: 0)` handles everything: touch-down tilts the card toward the finger and scales it to 0.98, an 8pt sideways move turns into a scrub where the full card width equals 180°, and a lift without movement is a tap.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Release commits when `predictedEndTranslation` projects past 90° in either direction, so a flick finishes the flip and a slow drag that stops short snaps back. Dragging past a full turn rubber-bands at 200°.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Each face darkens with `brightness` as it turns edge-on and hides past 90°; the back is pre-rotated by -180° so it lands unmirrored. The shadow slides opposite the lifted edge and widens mid-flip.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The angle accumulates (0, 180, 360...) so repeated flips keep rotating the same way; `isFlipped:` stays in sync in both directions.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: A soft impact fires as the visible face changes. Reduce Motion replaces the rotation with a crossfade that the drag still scrubs.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: **v2:** the card lifts 6% toward you at the edge-on point, sits on a layered shadow (a tight contact shadow plus a soft key shadow that slides off the raised edge), a soft-light band crosses each face as it turns, and the scrub rubber-bands past a half turn. Touch-down gives a light impact.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `style:` (`FlipCard.Style`) tunes `cornerRadius`, `shadow`/`shadowOpacity` (tripled in dark mode), `lift`, `pressScale`, `pressTilt`, and `shading`. `onFlip:` reports each committed flip. A disabled card dims and ignores touches.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The example is a vocabulary flashcard: a butter front with a heavy word and a sky back with the meaning. The preview shows the card alone, with no surrounding UI.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: For a full card screen with number masking and controls, see the Pro Card Details screen (`payment-card`).

title: Motion Card
description: A solid color card that tilts with the device's attitude through an exponential filter, with a fixed-light sheen and a layered shadow that slide as it turns. Press settles it flat and scales it down with a light impact, and Core Motion stops whenever the scene is not active.

contents.content: Attitude-driven card with a fixed-light sheen, tracking shadow, and press feedback.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Core Motion roll and pitch are measured relative to the pose at the moment updates start, so the card sits flat however the phone is held, then run through an exponential filter (15% per sample at 60Hz) that removes hand jitter without perceptible lag.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Motion starts on appear and whenever `scenePhase` becomes `.active`, and stops on disappear and in any other phase, so the sensors never run in the background. In the simulator, and with Reduce Motion, the card is static with a fixed light.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Pass `attitude:` (-1...1 per axis) to drive the tilt yourself for previews, tests, or the simulator; it replaces device motion entirely.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The specular highlight is an 11% white radial gradient whose center moves opposite the tilt, as a reflection of a fixed light would; the shadow slides the same way and widens with the tilt magnitude.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The card draws its own surface (`secondarySystemGroupedBackground`, 0.5pt hairline, continuous corners) under your content. Press scales to 0.98 with a light impact; a lift within 10pt runs `action` if one is set.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The motion source is a nested `@Observable` class marked `fileprivate`, because the macro's generated extension cannot see a `private` nested type.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: **v2:** the card draws a solid block (`style.fill`, tangerine by default) with dark ink, a soft-light sheen plus a faint far-side shade that follow a fixed light, and a two-layer shadow. Pressing settles the tilt halfway to flat, tightens the shadow, and scales to `pressScale`. Disabled cards desaturate.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `style:` (`MotionCard.Style`) sets `fill`, `foreground`, `sheen`, `shadowOpacity`, and `pressScale`; `cornerRadius` now defaults to 26.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The example is a film ticket with light seat numerals and perforation notches.

title: Parallax Card
description: An image card whose picture drifts slower than the scroll while a solid caption block drifts slower still, so the card reads in layers. Press lifts it with a deeper shadow and nudges the trailing glyph, and the caption is composed from eyebrow, title, metadata, and trailing glyph slots.

contents.content: Image card with two-layer scroll parallax, press-to-lift, and a slotted caption.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The drift is computed with `visualEffect` from `proxy.frame(in: .scrollView)`, so the card works inside any `ScrollView` or `List` without a named coordinate space. Outside a scroll view it renders static.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Three layers move at different rates: the image at `parallax`, the caption at a third of that, and the scrim scales from 1.3x tall at the viewport center to 0.9x at the edges, so the bottom reads tighter as the card leaves.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The image is oversized by `height * parallax` on each side and clipped, so no background shows at the extremes.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Pass `action:` to make the card a `Button`; the press style scales it to 1.02 and deepens the shadow with a fast press-in and a springy release. Without an action it keeps a resting shadow.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The caption is slots: `eyebrow` (uppercased, tracked), `title`, `metadata` (dot-separated row), and `trailingSymbol` (in a translucent circle). All text is white over the scrim, which is fine on light photos in both color schemes.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Reduce Motion disables the drift and the scrim scaling; the composition is unchanged.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: **v2:** the caption defaults to a solid inset block (`.block`) that drifts at a third of the picture's rate, with a heavy title, a dimmed metadata row, and the trailing glyph in an ink circle that nudges toward its arrow on press. `ParallaxCard.Style.scrim` restores white text over the tightening scrim.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `style:` (`ParallaxCard.Style`) sets `caption`, `captionFill`, `captionInk`, and `shadowOpacity`; `cornerRadius` now defaults to 26. The press state reaches the caption through the environment, so VoiceOver still reads the button label.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The example renders each picture as a flat composition (a color ground, a disc, a cropped giant word) with `ImageRenderer`; no photos ship with the piece.

title: Swipe Deck
description: A gesture-driven card stack: the top card follows the finger and swings from its base, a solid outcome badge fades in for the direction you are heading and locks at the threshold, the cards beneath rise as it leaves, and release past the threshold or a flick throws it left, right, or up.

contents.content: Swipeable card stack over Identifiable data. The deck removes the top item from `items` after each throw.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The deck is the source of truth for nothing: it removes the top item from the bound `items` array after each throw and reports the direction through `onSwipe`. Append items to keep the stack going, or watch the array run empty.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Directions use SwiftUI's `Edge` so the file stays self-contained: `.trailing` (swiped right), `.leading` (left), `.top` (up). Down is never committed; a downward drag springs back.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Commit is decided from `predictedEndTranslation`, so a flick throws even from a short drag. The horizontal threshold is 40% of the width, the upward one 30% of the height. A `.selection` tick fires the moment the drag crosses either, and a solid impact fires on the throw.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The card flies along its actual vector (drag plus velocity) for 1.6x the deck's larger dimension, then is removed without a transition while the next card springs up from 0.95 scale and 14pt lower.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Rotation is 14° per card width with a bottom anchor, so the card swings like it is pinned at the base. Reduce Motion drops the rotation and fades the card out in place instead of throwing it.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `swipe:` is a command binding: set it to a direction to throw programmatically (from buttons, a keyboard shortcut, or a preview loop); the deck resets it to nil. VoiceOver gets "Swipe right", "Swipe left", and "Swipe up" actions on the top card.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Give the deck an explicit frame; cards are sized to fill it.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: **v2:** outcome badges. While the top card heads left, right, or up, a solid badge (Skip, Keep, Save by default) fades and scales in for that direction and locks with a pop at the threshold. Cards further down sit in shade and brighten as they rise, and the top card's shadow deepens with the drag.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `style:` (`SwipeDeck.Style`) sets the three `SwipeDeck.Badge` values (title, symbol, fill, ink; nil hides one), `cornerRadius`, `shadowOpacity`, and `emptyMessage`, a dashed slot drawn when the deck runs out. `.plain` turns badges and the slot off. VoiceOver actions use the badge titles.

title: Commit Button
description: An async action button driven by one idle/loading/success/error/disabled phase: a signal capsule collapses to a spinning ring, closes it and blooms into a sage success block with a drawn check, or re-expands as a butter error block that shakes and doubles as retry.

contents.content: Async action button whose whole lifecycle is one bound `phase`.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `phase` is a `Binding` so the button can return itself to `.idle` after the success hold (`successHold`, default 900ms); everything else is set by you: `.loading` in the action, `.success` or `.error("message")` when the work finishes.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: States, all from `Style.standard`: idle is a signal capsule with dark ink; pressed squashes and darkens; loading collapses to a circle with an ink arc; success closes the arc, turns sage and draws the check, then, if you pass `successTitle` ("Saved"), blooms back into a sage capsule with an ink check disc; error re-expands as a butter block with an ink "!" disc, rolls the label to the message and shakes; disabled uses the raised color with muted ink.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Tapping in the error state fires the action again, so the message doubles as a retry (VoiceOver hears "Double tap to try again"). The button ignores taps while loading or succeeding without dimming.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `tint` and `errorTint` still work: they override the style fills and switch that state's ink to white. For full control pass a `Style` with your own fills, ink, height and font.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Reduce Motion crossfades the label, shortens the collapse and skips the shake offset; the haptics stay.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Need a slide-to-act confirmation with an amount and recipient? SwiftPieces Pro has the Send Money screen (`swipe-to-confirm`).

title: Elastic Button
description: A ButtonStyle that squashes toward the touch point, stretches with rubber-band resistance when dragged, deepens after a hold and snaps back with a spring. Optional solid surfaces (signal, block, raised) press into their own soft shadow and darken under the finger.

contents.content: Squash-and-stretch press for any `Button`. Apply with `.buttonStyle(.elastic)`, or `.buttonStyle(.elastic(.signal))` to also draw the surface.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: It is a `ButtonStyle`, so it works on any `Button`: `.buttonStyle(.elastic)` adds only the motion, `.buttonStyle(.elastic(.signal))` also draws the surface, and `.elastic(squash:bounce:haptics:style:)` tunes both.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `Style` presets come from the house palette: `.standard` (motion only, your label keeps its look), `.signal` for the one primary action, `.block(.lilac)` and the other blocks for secondary actions with dark ink, `.raised` for quiet ones. `radius`, `height` (never below 44) and `padding` are adjustable.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: States: at rest a drawn surface sits on a soft two-layer shadow; pressed it squashes toward the finger, darkens and the shadow flattens; after a 350ms hold it presses 0.03 deeper and darkens further with a soft impact; a drag past 44pt cancels the press with a soft impact; disabled surfaces switch to the raised color with muted ink instead of fading.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The touch point comes from a simultaneous zero-distance drag, so the squash leans 60% of the way toward the finger, the shape stretches along the drag axis with rubber-band resistance, and the offset follows at 35%. Release uses `.snappy` plus `bounce` as extra bounce.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Reduce Motion keeps the scale and darken but removes the lean, stretch and offset. Disabled buttons play no haptics.

description: Overlapping block-color avatars that fan apart on tap or hold with staggered springs, dissolve the +N pill into the hidden faces, and let a drag scrub across them: the avatar under the finger lifts, shows a name tag and ticks a haptic, and releasing selects it.

contents.content: Avatar group that expands into a selectable fan.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Tap toggles the fan; a 300ms hold fans it and keeps the touch live so you can scrub. While fanned, the avatar under the finger lifts (scale 1.18, a 4pt rise, soft shadow), shows its full name in an inverted tag above, bolds its first name below, and ticks `.selection` per crossing. Releasing on it calls `onSelect` and collapses; releasing a hold on empty space leaves the fan open; a tap on empty space closes it.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Initials sit on solid house blocks with dark ink, picked by a stable FNV-1a hash of the name. `Style` sets the block list, ink, the cut-out `ring` (match it to the surface behind the stack), the "+N" pill and the name tag.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Every name is in the hierarchy at all times. Collapsed, avatars past `max` sit hidden at the "+N" pill's position, so on expand they emerge from where the pill dissolves. Springs stagger 35ms per avatar, reversed on collapse.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The tag draws 34pt above the avatars and first names 24pt below while fanned (the frame grows for the names only), so leave room above the stack.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `images` is a parallel array; it may be shorter than `names`, and `nil` entries fall back to initials.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Reduce Motion removes the stagger and the lift; the hovered avatar shows a ring instead. VoiceOver reads the collapsed stack as one element ("Priya Raman, Jonas Weber, and 3 more", double tap to expand) and each avatar as its own button once fanned.

contents.content: Hold to confirm. The label inverts as the fill passes under it; letting go or dragging off rewinds.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The track is a raised capsule with an ink puck holding the symbol. While held, a solid fill sweeps from under the puck across the track, driven by a `TimelineView`; an ink copy of the label and puck is masked to the fill, so both invert as it passes.

contents.heading: notes

contents.heading: notes

contents.heading: notes

description: A countdown ring you set by dragging its knob around like the Timer dial, with a tick per step and a heavier detent every 5s. A solid block ring over a minute-tick scale, light display numerals, a breathing signal warning zone, a sage finish, and a determinate progress mode.

title: Activity Heatmap
description: A streak calendar for habit, fitness, study and journaling apps: weeks of days drawn in one Canvas as rounded cells in solid steps from a pale red mix up to pure red, laid out by the locale's first weekday with month labels on their week columns, a light streak numeral that stays alive until midnight beside the longest run and active days, a scrub that lifts the day under your finger with a callout and a haptic tick per day, sideways scrolling that opens on today when the weeks outgrow the width, and VoiceOver that steps day by day or plays the weeks as an audio graph.

contents.content: A calendar heatmap of daily activity with the current streak, a scrub callout and full VoiceOver support. Columns are weeks, oldest leading and newest trailing, and rows are weekdays in the calendar's order, so Monday-first regions get Monday on top. Each day is one rounded cell: level 0 is an empty field and levels 1 to 4 are solid steps of the accent mixed into the ground, up to the pure accent. Drag sideways across the grid, or press and move, to read any day, and tap to select one; vertical swipes still scroll the screen. When the weeks outgrow the width the grid scrolls sideways and a short hold starts the reading instead. The cells are drawn in one `Canvas` and hit-tested by geometry, so a year of days stays light.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Pass activity keyed by day as `[Date: Double]` or `[Date: Int]`. Each key lands on the day it falls on in the calendar's time zone, so exact timestamps work and several entries on one day add up. Zero, negative and non-finite values count as no activity. If you store days as midnight UTC, pass a calendar whose time zone is UTC.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Columns are weeks, oldest leading and newest trailing, and rows are weekdays in the calendar's order: the person's own first weekday by default, so Monday-first regions get Monday on top. Days are stepped from noon, so daylight saving changes and leap days never skip or double a cell. Month labels sit above the first week of each month, and the weekday labels mark Monday, Wednesday and Friday on whichever rows they fall.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Level 0 is the empty field. Levels 1 to 4 are solid steps of the accent mixed into the ground (pale on light, deep on dark, further apart with Increase Contrast), up to the pure accent, never transparency. `.automatic` splits the non-zero days in view into quartiles, so one huge day does not wash out the rest and the busiest day always takes the top shade. `.thresholds([1, 3, 6, 10])` sets the minimum for each level; fewer than four spread over the shades, so `.thresholds([1])` draws a done or not done habit in the full accent.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The current streak counts back from today and stays alive until midnight while today has nothing yet. It looks back through all of your data, so a streak that began before the first visible week is counted in full; the longest streak and the active days cover the visible weeks. With `.thresholds`, the first value is what counts as active. `ActivityHeatmap.summary(of:)` returns the same figures for a widget or a reminder.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Drag sideways across the grid, or press and move, and the day under the finger lifts with a callout (date, value and its shade) and a selection tick for each new day. Vertical swipes that start on the grid still scroll the screen or move a sheet. Tap a day to select it and tap it again to clear it.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: With a `selection` binding, a scrub moves the selection live and release keeps it; setting it from outside selects that day and scrolls it into view. Without a binding, a scrub shows the callout only while the finger is down, and a tap keeps it.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Cells grow to fill the width up to `Style.maximumCellSize`. When the weeks would make them smaller than `Style.minimumCellSize`, the grid scrolls sideways, opens on today and comes to rest on whole weeks; sideways swipes scroll it and a quarter-second hold starts reading instead.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Today wears a ring in the text color, and days after the end date are left out. `endDate` shows an earlier range; `nil` (the default) follows today and moves on by itself at midnight or when the time zone changes.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The cells fill in with a quick wave once, a day whose value changes pops, and the streak numeral rolls to its new value. Reduce Motion drops the wave, the pop and the lift's spring.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: VoiceOver reads the heatmap as one adjustable element: "Activity, last 20 weeks. Current streak 12 days. Longest 31 days. Active 86 days." Swipe up or down to move a day (the value reads "Tuesday, September 30, 45 min"), use the Previous week and Next week actions, and the escape gesture clears the selection. It also offers the days as an audio graph. With a hardware keyboard, the up and down arrows move a day and left and right move a week.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: While your data loads, apply `.redacted(reason: .placeholder)`: the grid keeps its shape in empty cells and the figures redact. With no activity in view the summary reads "No activity yet".

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Dynamic Type scales the streak, the figures and the labels; the summary stacks at large sizes and the grid labels stop growing before they crowd the rows, while cells keep their size. Right to left, the weeks run from the right, newest on the left.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `Style` sets the accent, the ground the shades are mixed into (set it to the surface the heatmap sits on), the empty, text, secondary and callout colors, the cell radius and spacing, the smallest and largest cell, and the numeral size. `Style.fill(level:)` gives the same shades for your own day details. `Messages` replaces any line of built-in copy, and `valueLabel` names your unit, for example minutes formatted as a `Measurement`.

title: Odometer
description: A number whose digits roll on individual slots like a mechanical counter, carrying from the low digits up so unchanged digits never move, with softened slot edges while rolling, dimmed decimals, a separate sign, a solid delta block, and a dashed loading state.

contents.content: Slot-machine number with a single spring-driven `Animatable` value behind every digit.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: One `Animatable` number drives every slot. Each digit's roll is derived from that number and carries upward only while the digit below passes 9, so higher digits stay perfectly still until a carry reaches them. While a digit is between faces its slot edges soften, like a drum turning behind a window. The roll runs on `.smooth` with a duration that grows gently with the size of the change; there is no per-frame loop.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: The layout (grouping separators, decimal separator, currency symbol) is read from the formatted target once per change. Use plain decimal or currency styles; compact notation such as `1.2K` will not match the rolled digits. Leading symbols always show, and the number never gives up width to the delta pill.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: Decimals and their separator are dimmed by default. The sign is its own glyph and slides in or out at the zero crossing. After each change a solid delta block shows the signed amount for 1.6 s: sage for up, tangerine for down, ink text.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `Style` sets `up`, `down`, `ink`, `muted`, `dimsFraction`, and `tintsWhileRolling` (tints the digits until the roll settles; best on dark grounds).

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: `isLoading` swaps every digit for a dash; the first real value rolls up from zero. Reduce Motion replaces the roll with a short ease.

contents.heading: notes
contents.content: VoiceOver reads the final formatted value only, never the intermediate frames. Apply `.font` to the `Odometer` (light weights suit it); slot sizes are measured from that font.
